turns.text: What do you remember about your very first morning after arriving in Beidahuang from Shanghai? What did you see, hear, and feel when you woke up?

The first morning, I woke up shivering before the sun even rose. My breath fogged in the air above my blanket. The room was crowded, the walls thin, and I could hear the heavy breathing and restless shifting of the other girls. My back ached from the hard board bed. I could smell damp straw and something sour, maybe from someone’s shoes. When I stepped outside, the wind hit my face sharp and cold, nothing like the wet warmth of Shanghai. My hands went numb as I tried to wash my face at the pump, the water biting my skin. The fields stretched out flat and gray, no buildings, just endless mud and the faint outline of trees. I felt small, almost erased. The silence was bigger than I was used to—no traffic, no shouting, just the wind and the distant sound of someone coughing. I wanted to go home, but I knew that was impossible.

The way you describe the cold, the silence, and the endless fields makes it feel so isolating. You mentioned the sour smell in the room and the ache from the board bed—how did those small discomforts affect your mood or your sense of belonging in those early days?

Those little things—like the scratchy straw poking through the thin blanket, or the way my back always hurt—made everything feel temporary, like I was just a visitor, not someone who belonged. I kept thinking about my bed at home, the softness, the warmth, the smell of my mother’s cooking drifting through the apartment. Here, every morning started with those small irritations, and it made me impatient and irritable. I was surrounded by other city kids, but we all kept to ourselves at first, each of us nursing our own homesickness. The discomforts were constant reminders that this wasn’t my life, not really, and it made me want to withdraw even more. I think it took weeks before I stopped flinching at the smells or the cold and started to accept that this was normal now.

I can still feel the way my skin crawled when I lay down at night, the straw shifting underneath me, sometimes scratching my legs through the thin sheet. It was hard to sleep, not just from the ache in my back but from the sounds—sniffling, someone quietly crying, the creak of the boards. Every time I closed my eyes, I pictured my old pillow, my sisters fighting over space, the hum of the city outside our window. Here, everything was unfamiliar, and those little discomforts made it seem like I was holding my breath all day. I didn’t talk much to the others at first. I didn’t trust that anyone felt the same way, even though I could see the tiredness in their faces. The cold, the smells, the roughness—they all pressed in, making it hard to remember who I was before I got on the train. I felt like a guest in my own body.

The way you describe feeling like a guest in your own body is striking—it sounds like the physical environment deeply affected your sense of self. You mentioned hearing someone quietly crying at night; do you remember a particular moment when you or someone else finally broke the silence and shared how you were feeling?

One night, maybe a month in, I woke up to someone sobbing—not just sniffling, but really crying, muffled into her blanket. At first, everyone pretended to sleep, but the sound kept going. I remember sitting up and, without thinking, asking if she was okay. My voice sounded strange in the dark. For a moment, no one said anything, but then a few others started talking too. It was like a dam broke. We all admitted we missed home, that we hated the cold, even that we were scared. We whispered into the night, trading little stories about our families, our favorite foods, things we’d brought from home. After that, it was easier—we started sharing more, even laughing sometimes when someone complained about the pump or the food. That was the first time I felt less alone, like maybe I didn’t have to hold my breath all the time.

That night changed something for me. I remember my hands shaking, not from cold but from the relief of finally saying what I’d been hiding. I could hear the others’ voices, soft and tired, but honest. Someone passed around a scrap of candy she’d saved, and we all took a tiny piece. I clung to that sweetness on my tongue, letting it remind me of home. The next morning, when we went out to the fields, I noticed we walked a little closer together. We still didn’t talk much in front of the locals or the leaders, but in the evenings, we started whispering, sharing memories and small hopes. It didn’t make the work easier, but it made me feel like I had a place, even if it was just a narrow corner of that cold, crowded room.

The image of sharing a single scrap of candy and walking closer together the next morning is so vivid. You mentioned that you still didn’t talk much in front of the locals or the leaders—did you ever feel tension or misunderstanding between you and the people who had always lived there?

There was definitely tension. The locals saw us as useless at first—soft city kids who didn’t know how to hold a hoe or even tie up our shoes properly for the mud. Sometimes they laughed when we stumbled or blistered our hands, and I could feel their eyes on us, measuring and judging. I remember one woman shaking her head as I tried to carry water from the well, spilling half of it before I got back. She muttered something about “delicate hands,” and I felt my face burn. It wasn’t just the work, though. We spoke differently, dressed differently, even ate differently when we could. They thought we were spoiled, and maybe we were compared to their lives. At times, they seemed resentful that we’d come at all, as if we were intruders in their hardship. I wanted to prove myself, but I also felt a stubborn pride—like I shouldn’t have to apologize for the life I’d had before. That made it hard for either side to really understand the other.

I remember watching the way they moved—steady, practiced, almost silent in the fields. Their hands were scarred but sure, and their faces didn’t give much away. When I tried to copy them, I always felt clumsy, my feet sinking too deep into the mud, my shoulders burning after an hour. Sometimes a local would correct me with a sharp word or a quick demonstration, but there was no warmth in it. At meal times, we kept to our own tables, trading glances but not words. I could sense their frustration, maybe even anger, that we were there because of politics, not by choice. I heard them joke that we’d all run home crying if we could. There were moments when I wanted to shout back, to defend myself, but I never did. I just worked until my hands bled, hoping that would speak for me. Even then, I knew I would always be an outsider.

The image of working until your hands bled, hoping your effort would speak for you, is haunting. You mentioned the locals sometimes corrected you without warmth—was there ever a moment, even a small one, when someone from the village showed you unexpected kindness or understanding?

There was one morning when my fingers were cracked and raw from the cold and the work. I was struggling to tie bundles of reeds, fumbling with the twine. An older woman came over—she didn’t say anything at first, just watched me for a while. Then she knelt beside me, took my hands, and showed me a different way to loop the twine so it wouldn’t cut so deep. Her hands were rough, but gentle, and she wrapped my fingers in a scrap of cloth she’d brought in her pocket. She didn’t smile or speak much, but she nodded once, like an approval. After that, she’d sometimes leave a bit of ointment or a piece of cloth near my spot in the shed. We never really talked, but I started to look for her in the fields, and it made those hours feel a little less endless.

The memory of her hands—strong, warm compared to mine—stayed with me. I remember the way she pressed the cloth into my palm, almost as if she was embarrassed to be seen helping. I never asked her for anything, and she never asked about my life in Shanghai. It was just these quiet exchanges: a nod, a gesture, a small kindness left where no one else would notice. Sometimes I would see her watching me from across the field, her face unreadable, but I knew she saw how hard I was trying. Those moments didn’t erase the distance between us, but they softened it. I started to understand that kindness could be silent, and that sometimes it came from the people you least expected.

It’s moving how you describe those quiet exchanges—how kindness didn’t need words. Thinking back on those moments, do you feel they changed the way you thought about home, or about what it means to belong somewhere?
